claims.text: The untreated starting composite contains interconnected W ligaments or dispersed W particles in a Cu matrix.
A roughly 200 nm Mo or Re coating can be deposited on W by PVD before hot isostatic pressing with Cu.
The proposed processing creates a W–Mo/Re–Cu interface.
The refractory interlayer inhibits direct W–Cu contact.
The Mo or Re interlayer slows interdiffusion between W and Cu.
Slower interdiffusion reduces microvoid nucleation at the W–Cu interface.
The interlayer helps maintain a dense W–Cu interface.
The interlayer mitigates phase separation at high temperature and under irradiation.
Reduced interdiffusion, voiding, and phase separation retain or enhance the composite's effective thermal conductivity.
After matched heat and irradiation exposure, the coated composite will have significantly fewer interfacial voids than the uncoated composite.
After matched exposure, the coated composite may retain thermal conductivity 10–15% above that of the untreated composite.
W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based heat sinks operate in a high-temperature, high-heat-flux, irradiation environment.
Heat flux above 10 MW/m² and moderate ion irradiation are representative service conditions for these joints.
Untreated W–Cu composites typically undergo interfacial diffusion at elevated temperature and under irradiation.
Untreated W–Cu composites typically develop interfacial voids that degrade overall thermal conductivity.
Incomplete coating coverage may compromise barrier performance.
High neutron flux or prolonged exposure above approximately 1000 °C may compromise the barrier.
The long-term stability of the proposed barrier under repeated thermal cycling and high-fluence neutron irradiation has not been comprehensively demonstrated.

contradictions.description: The stated service boundary requires heat flux greater than 10 MW/m², whereas the proposed test uses approximately 10 MW/m² and therefore may not enter the claimed regime.
